clue.text: Stuart has quarter-pint with Fish, caricaturist

parts.note: James was the name of Stuart kings, so a Stuart can be James
a gill is an old measure equal to a quarter of a pint
the ray is a flat fish

explanation.surface: A Stuart monarch shares a small drink with a fishy companion and a cartoonist.
explanation.walkthrough: Gillray was the great Georgian satirical cartoonist; the capital F on 'Fish' pretends it is a surname.
explanation.definitionFit: James Gillray was an English satirical artist famous for political cartoons of the late eighteenth century.

clue.text: Spring-time woollies?

parts.note: knitted pullovers, read whimsically as things or people that spring and leap

explanation.surface: Light knitwear for wearing in the spring season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring-time' suggests the season, but those who spring are leapers, and pullovers carry the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitted woollen pullovers are called by the same word as people who leap.

clue.text: American inventor made a dash for the West End

annotationWithheld.why: American inventor made a dash for the West End (5): MORSE fits 'American inventor' and Morse code's dash, but no parse found explains 'for the West End'
annotationWithheld.clue: American inventor made a dash for the West End

clue.text: Inefficient still?

definitions.meaning: without any shift or movement, hence motionless

explanation.surface: Asking whether something is still not working well.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second sense as SHIFT-LESS: with no shift, nothing moves, so it is still.
explanation.definitionFit: Lazy and lacking resource is the dictionary sense; read jokingly it is without movement, hence motionless.

clue.text: Tree causes awkward, lie — sign of the "times"

indicators.note: awkward means clumsy or out of shape, so the letters of the word lie are rearranged

parts.note: the multiplication symbol, read as times, is an X

explanation.surface: A tree tells an awkward lie, typical of the times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' turns LIE into ILE; 'sign of the times' is a familiar phrase, but here it is the multiplication sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilex is the genus of holly, also used for the holm oak.

clue.text: Call for the letters?

parts.note: a bugle call at the end of the day, read as the final mail collection

explanation.surface: Someone asks for correspondence to be brought.
explanation.walkthrough: The military bugle call sounded at dusk and at funerals is reread as the last collection of mail from a box.
explanation.definitionFit: The final bugle call of the day shares its name with the last mail collection.

clue.text: Besides, Niagara's beginning to rise

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters are read upward, from bottom to top
the beginning of the word is its opening five letters taken in order

explanation.surface: Moreover, the start of Niagara is going up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' takes NIAGA from the start of Niagara; 'to rise' turns it upward in this down light to read AGAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Again can mean furthermore or in addition, as besides does.

clue.text: Catch in agreement?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a loophole is hidden in an agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' looks like a hidden snag in a deal, but it means to catch an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract a disease is to catch it, and a binding agreement is a legal contract.

clue.text: Untold wealth in such a hoard

definitions.meaning: not told to anyone, kept hidden
a stash kept hidden from others

explanation.surface: An untold fortune lies in a certain treasure trove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Untold wealth' reads as a phrase meaning immense riches; split it, and untold means not revealed, while wealth is kept in a hidden hoard.
explanation.definitionFit: Untold means kept hidden; wealth stashed where no one knows is a hidden hoard.

clue.text: Strict disciplinarians made Kingsley the editor — odd set "

parts.note: Kingsley Martin was the long-serving editor of the New Statesman

indicators.note: odd suggests the word set appears in a strange, rearranged form

explanation.surface: Martinets made the editor Kingsley a peculiar collection of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' turns SET into ETS. Kingsley Martin edited the New Statesman magazine from 1930 to 1960; solvers expecting Kingsley Amis will be misled.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a rigid enforcer of rules, named after a strict seventeenth-century French drillmaster.

clue.text: Got up out of bed perhaps

definitions.meaning: past tense of rise, to stand or leave bed
a single flower taken from a garden bed

explanation.surface: Someone climbed from their bed in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second half as A ROSE: a single bloom plucked out of a flower bed, not a sleeper rising.
explanation.definitionFit: Got up is the past tense of rise; a rose is a flower that might be picked from a garden bed.

clue.text: They happened to have seen TV variety.

indicators.note: variety implies a mixed assortment, so these letters come in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: People recount having watched a variety show on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' looks like a TV genre but it signals the anagram of SEEN TV.
explanation.definitionFit: Events are occurrences, things that took place.

clue.text: Miss? Not Lily!

parts.note: an unmarried woman who works a spinning wheel, unlike the lilies of the field that toil not, neither do they spin

explanation.surface: A question about whether a young woman is called Lily.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sermon on the Mount says the lilies of the field 'toil not, neither do they spin'; one who spins is therefore no lily, and an old maid.
explanation.definitionFit: An unmarried woman is traditionally a spinster, originally a woman who spun thread for a living.

clue.text: Woodcutter visiting Dingley Dell

definitions.meaning: a person who cuts wood with a saw
a Pickwick Papers character who visits Wardle's home at Christmas

explanation.surface: A lumberjack calls in at a picturesque country spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Dingley Dell is Mr Wardle's farm in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, where the medical student Bob Sawyer visits at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: One who saws timber is a woodcutter; Bob Sawyer is a Dickens character who turns up at Wardle's Dingley Dell.

clue.text: Showing craft without deck building-very badly made

indicators.note: without means outside, so one piece is placed around the other

parts.note: craft is cunning, so showing craft means sly

indicators.note: building means constructing, so the letters of the word deck are put together anew

explanation.surface: A boat built with no deck was made very poorly, with some cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' suggests a boat but means guile; 'building' rearranges the deck letters, and 'without' wraps the cunning word around them.
explanation.definitionFit: Wickedly can mean extremely or terribly, so very badly.

clue.text: Has "ordered factory to make a walking-stick

indicators.note: ordered means arranged afresh, so the letters of the preceding word are reshuffled

parts.note: a plant is an industrial works

explanation.surface: Someone has commanded a factory to manufacture walking canes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' seems to be a command to the factory, but it rearranges HAS into ASH.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashplant is a walking cane cut from an ash sapling.

clue.text: Left clumsy fool holding one case

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one piece goes inside the other
clumsy means awkwardly made, so the letters of the word fool are rearranged

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: An awkward idiot left carrying a single bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb, but is the nautical side; 'clumsy' scrambles the fool and 'holding' puts the Roman one inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A portfolio is a flat case for carrying papers or drawings.

clue.text: Old minstrel has day abroad going round wild glen

indicators.note: going round means surrounding, so the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: jour is the French word for day

indicators.note: wild means unruly, so the letters of the word glen are rearranged

explanation.surface: A medieval minstrel spends a day overseas wandering a wild valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' says to use French for day; 'wild' scrambles glen, and 'going round' sets the French word around the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A jongleur was a travelling medieval entertainer who sang and recited.

clue.text: Ammunition for sportsmen — county, of high degree

parts.note: Bucks is the abbreviation for Buckinghamshire, an English county
hot means at a high temperature, many degrees on the thermometer

explanation.surface: Shooting cartridges for country gentlemen of a county family of high rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of high degree' suggests social rank, but means temperature. Buckinghamshire is a county north-west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckshot is the coarse lead shot loaded into cartridges for hunting game.

clue.text: Barely sufficient for Hamlet's quietus

parts.note: Hamlet says a man might his quietus make with a bare dagger, the bare small blade

explanation.surface: Something only just enough to bring about the Prince of Denmark's end.
explanation.walkthrough: In the 'To be or not to be' speech Hamlet says one might 'his quietus make with a bare bodkin'; 'Barely' plays on that bare.
explanation.definitionFit: A short pointed dagger is all Hamlet says is needed to end one's life.

clue.text: Harangued leader of opposition-trade reform

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter
reform means reshape, so the letters of the following word are rearranged

explanation.surface: The head of the Opposition railed about reforming trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' looks like a political policy, but it is the anagram signal on trade, following the opening letter of opposition.
explanation.definitionFit: To harangue is to deliver a long forceful speech, as one who orated did.

clue.text: One rising and shining bright and early

definitions.text: One rising and shining bright and early

parts.words: One rising and shining bright and early
parts.note: an early riser full of sunny energy, reread as a heavenly body that rises at dawn

explanation.surface: Someone who gets up keen and cheerful at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise and shine' is a wake-up call; here the one rising and shining is the morning star or the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The morning star, Venus, or the sun is the body seen bright at dawn.

clue.text: Horse-training becomes habit, with time

parts.note: a habit is a garment, as in a riding habit, so dress
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Equestrian schooling becomes a fixed habit over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: A riding habit is a woman's riding outfit, which suits the equestrian surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the art of schooling a horse in precise, controlled movements.

clue.text: Animal's.deadly sin

definitions.meaning: one of the seven capital vices, idleness

explanation.surface: A creature's fatal moral failing.
explanation.definitionFit: The sloth is a slow tree-dwelling mammal, and idleness is one of the seven deadly sins.

clue.text: Irish county cricket side lay in ruins

parts.note: the off side is one half of a cricket field

indicators.note: in ruins means wrecked, so the letters of the word lay are scrambled

explanation.surface: A cricket team from an Irish county was left devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the off side is the half of the field facing the batsman's bat; 'in ruins' turns LAY into ALY.
explanation.definitionFit: Offaly is a county in the Irish midlands.

clue.text: Ward off VAT collector? without hesitation!

annotationWithheld.why: Ward off VAT collector? without hesitation! (5): AVERT fits 'Ward off', but the only parse found, ER inside VAT, needs VAT rearranged with no word to signal it
annotationWithheld.clue: Ward off VAT collector? without hesitation!

clue.text: Play parts in book

definitions.meaning: the main divisions of a stage play
a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: Taking roles in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Acts of the Apostles is a book of the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: A play divides into acts, and Acts is the fifth book of the New Testament.

clue.text: White House has some big looking-glasses

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: The American president's residence contains several large mirrors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White House' wants to be Washington; it is a snow house.
explanation.definitionFit: An Eskimo snow hut is a dwelling made of white blocks of packed snow.

clue.text: Out of prison _confinement ten riot-get fine_

parts.note: ex as a prefix means former, so out of prison as in ex-con
a cell is a place of confinement

indicators.note: riot suggests disorder, so the letters of the word ten are scrambled

explanation.surface: A prisoner released after a jail riot is told to pay a fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riot' turns TEN into ENT; 'fine' looks like a penalty but means very good.
explanation.definitionFit: Excellent means extremely good, as fine does in praise.

clue.text: He aims to hit Rebecca's vulgar nose

parts.note: Becky Sharp, Rebecca, is the heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair, with the possessive S
hooter is a slang word for the nose

explanation.surface: Someone is out to punch a woman named Rebecca on her coarse nose.
explanation.walkthrough: Becky (Rebecca) Sharp is the scheming heroine of Vanity Fair; HOOTER is British slang for a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A marksman with a rifle aims at targets and seldom misses.
